subtype: Approach: asks what a good enough choice would be and what reversing it would cost [Revision]
passage: I'm Hafsa, and Divyansh and I were in the same first-year batch. For a whole week he agonised over the sports elective: badminton, swimming or yoga. He made lists. He asked seniors. He went to see the pool twice. On Thursday evening I found him outside the sports office staring at the notice board. Then I watched his face change. He tapped a line on the notice and read it out: "Students may switch electives in the first two weeks." He laughed at himself. "So if I hate it, I just switch. Why am I treating this like marriage?" He wrote "badminton" on the form in about ten seconds and handed it in. That night he was back in the library, working on the coding assignment he'd been putting off.

qa.q: What did the line on the notice board say?
qa.a: "Students may switch electives in the first two weeks."

qa.q: What might Divyansh have felt when he laughed at himself?
qa.a: He seemed relieved and a bit embarrassed at how much worry he'd put into a choice he could undo.

qa.q: What else could Divyansh ask himself before future choices?
qa.a: Whether the choice can be reversed and what that would cost; if it's cheap to undo, choose a good-enough option quickly.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see the change in Divyansh?
qa.a: Hafsa seems amused and glad to see him drop the agonising and get back to the assignment.

grounding: Realising the choice can be changed later, a student picks a reasonable option and spends the time saved on something more important.

subtype: Approach: asks what a good enough choice would be and what reversing it would cost [Revision]
passage:
Monday: Arnab had to pick a foreign language for his second year: German, French or Japanese. He opened eleven tabs of comparisons and asked Gautam, his roommate, for the third time which had "better scope".

Wednesday: Still undecided, he found the course handbook in his inbox. Gautam pointed at page four: "Language can be changed at the end of the first term with no penalty." Arnab sat back. "So the worst case is I lose one term of French and switch." He picked French because the class timing fit his lab schedule, closed the tabs and sent the form.

The next Monday: Arnab spent the evening he'd have used for comparing on his circuits project, which was due first.

qa.q: When can the language be changed, according to the handbook?
qa.a: At the end of the first term with no penalty.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel once he saw page four?
qa.a: He felt relieved and lighter, realising the worst case was small and the choice didn't have to be perfect.

qa.q: Which choice helped Arnab most, and why?
qa.a: Asking what reversing the choice would cost; once it was low, a good-enough option was enough.

qa.q: How might Gautam see Arnab's decision?
qa.a: Gautam is probably relieved not to be asked about "scope" a fourth time.

grounding: A student realises a choice can be reversed, picks a reasonable option and uses the saved time on work that matters more.

subtype: Approach: sets a deadline and a limit on how many options to consider [Revision]
passage: Siddiq had moved to Madrid for work and wanted to learn Spanish properly. For a month he'd looked at language schools: evening classes, weekend classes, online tutors, conversation clubs. Twenty-three bookmarks. Every Sunday he said, "Next week I'll decide." At lunch on Monday, his colleague Javier asked how the classes were going. Siddiq admitted he hadn't started. That evening he made a rule. He picked three schools near his flat or office, no more. He wrote on a sticky note: "Choose by Sunday. Good enough is good enough." He visited two on Wednesday and called the third on Thursday. On Saturday he signed up for Tuesday and Thursday evenings at the school ten minutes from the office. On Monday he told Javier, "Hola. Classes start tomorrow."

qa.q: How many bookmarks had Siddiq saved?
qa.a: Twenty-three bookmarks.

qa.q: How did Siddiq feel when he admitted he hadn't started?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed, since every Sunday he'd said he would decide the next week.

qa.q: What made Siddiq's new method work?
qa.a: Limiting himself to three options and a Sunday deadline turned an endless search into a small task with an end.

qa.q: How might Javier see Siddiq's news on Monday?
qa.a: Javier would likely be amused and pleased that Siddiq finally started, and might offer to practise Spanish with him.

grounding: A young professional limits the search to three options with a Sunday deadline, turning an open search into a task with an end.

subtype: Approach: sets a deadline and a limit on how many options to consider [Revision]
passage: At the school where Binita worked in administration, the staff canteen contract was ending, and she had been asked to pick a new caterer. For two weeks she'd collected menus, prices and reviews from nine caterers and felt more stuck each day. Her colleague Samir found her in the office on Tuesday with papers all over the table. "Pick three," he said. "Any three that meet the basics. Decide by Sunday." Binita frowned, then nodded. She crossed out six that were too far away or too expensive. On Thursday the three remaining sent sample lunches, and the teachers tasted them in the staffroom. By Friday afternoon she had chosen the one the teachers liked most. She put the other menus in a drawer and felt the tightness in her shoulders go.

qa.q: How many caterers had Binita collected information from?
qa.a: Nine caterers.

qa.q: What does the tightness leaving Binita's shoulders suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt relieved once the endless search turned into a decision.

qa.q: What could Binita do if the new caterer doesn't work out?
qa.a: Go back to the other two shortlisted menus in the drawer, rather than restarting with all nine.

qa.q: How might the teachers see the tasting on Thursday?
qa.a: The teachers would likely enjoy being asked and feel their opinions counted in the choice.

grounding: A young professional limits the options to three and decides by a set day, turning an open search into a task with an end.

subtype: Approach: uses a trusted friend to break the tie [Action]
passage: In the nurses' rest room during the night shift, Rekha scrolled between two photos for the hundredth time. Flat A: near the hospital, small, noisy road. Flat B: bigger, quiet, forty minutes by bus. She'd visited both twice. She'd made lists. The owners wanted an answer by morning. Sabina, who had shared a room with her in nursing college for three years, came in with two cups of tea. "Still?" "I can't choose. You choose." Sabina laughed, then saw she meant it. "Okay. You hate early buses. You fall asleep anywhere, even with noise. You always say you want more time to sleep after nights. Flat A." Rekha let out a long breath. "Flat A." She messaged the owner before the tea cooled.

qa.q: How long is the bus ride from Flat B?
qa.a: Forty minutes by bus.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when Sabina chose Flat A?
qa.a: She felt relieved; her long breath showed the loop was finally over.

qa.q: Why did asking Sabina work so well?
qa.a: Sabina knew Rekha's habits, like hating early buses and sleeping through noise, so Sabina could decide in a way Rekha trusted.

qa.q: What is it like for Sabina to be asked to decide?
qa.a: Sabina may feel surprised at first, then trusted, and careful to choose based on what Sabina knows of Rekha.

grounding: Stuck between two flats, she asks a friend who knows her habits to choose, and handing over the tie-break ends the loop.

subtype: Approach: uses a trusted friend to break the tie [Action]
passage:
Hi Siddharth,

I need a favour, and it's a weird one. I've been going back and forth between two flats for ten days and I'm stuck.

Flat 1: near the metro, fourth floor, no lift, gets great morning light.
Flat 2: ground floor, a garden, twenty minutes' walk to the metro, a bit dark inside.

I've made pro-and-con lists, visited both twice and asked my sister, who picked one and then said "or the other one". I'm going in circles.

You've known me since school. You know how I am in the mornings, how much I care about light, whether I'll really use a garden. So please just choose. Whatever you say, I'll sign on Friday. I trust you more than my lists right now.

Ankita

qa.q: What does Flat 2 have?
qa.a: A garden, on the ground floor, twenty minutes' walk to the metro, and a bit dark inside.

qa.q: How is Ankita feeling about the decision?
qa.a: Ankita feels stuck and tired of going in circles, and trusts Siddharth more than the lists right now.

qa.q: What makes handing the choice to Siddharth a sensible step?
qa.a: Siddharth knows Ankita's habits from school, so Siddharth's choice can end the loop in a way Ankita will accept and sign on Friday.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel getting this email?
qa.a: Siddharth might feel flattered by the trust and a bit responsible, wanting to choose well.

grounding: Stuck between two flats, the writer asks a friend who knows those habits to choose, and handing over the tie-break ends the loop.

subtype: Approach: enjoys making plans more than doing the work [Thinking]
passage:
Shreya: made a new study chart!! 🎨 colour-coded by subject, with stickers for each chapter
Divyansh: that's like your 4th chart this month
Shreya: 5th actually. this one has a tracker column too
Divyansh: how many chapters have you ticked
Shreya: …
Shreya: zero
Divyansh: 😬
Shreya: ok wait. I think I know why. making charts feels good. like I'm already doing something. reading chemistry feels bad at the start
Shreya: so I keep making charts instead
Divyansh: so what now
Shreya: no new chart for 2 weeks. first chapter tonight, 30 mins, then I get to put ONE sticker
Divyansh: deal. send pic of sticker
Shreya: 🙂

qa.q: How many study charts had Shreya made this month?
qa.a: The 5th chart, with a tracker column too.

qa.q: Why does Shreya keep making charts, in Shreya's own words?
qa.a: Making charts feels good and like progress, while starting chemistry feels bad, so the charts are a way to avoid that uncomfortable start.

qa.q: What small step did Shreya choose, and why might it help?
qa.a: One 30-minute chapter tonight before any sticker, which ties the good feeling to real work.

qa.q: How does Divyansh see Shreya's charts?
qa.a: Divyansh seems amused but honest, gently pointing out that no chapters are done.

grounding: A teenager realises that elaborate study charts feel like progress while the chapters stay unread.

subtype: Approach: enjoys making plans more than doing the work [Thinking]
passage: In the small town of Bhuj, Noor's desk was covered in study plans. There was a weekly one, a monthly one, and a big one on chart paper with every chapter in a different colour. Her cousin Aparna, visiting for the holidays, whistled. "These are beautiful. How far have you got?" Noor opened her mouth, then shut it. She looked at the chart. Not one chapter was ticked. "I spend an hour making the plan and I feel like I've studied," she said slowly. "It's nice. Colouring is easy. The actual history chapter is hard, so I make another plan instead." Aparna sat on the bed. "So?" Noor put the felt pens in a drawer. "So tomorrow, no pens. Just chapter one."

qa.q: What was on the big chart paper plan?
qa.a: Every chapter in a different colour.

qa.q: What did Noor realise about why she kept planning?
qa.a: She realised planning felt easy and pleasant, like studying, while the actual chapter felt hard, so she avoided it.

qa.q: What else could Noor try so planning doesn't replace studying?
qa.a: Allow herself only five minutes of planning, then start a chapter straight away and tick it only when done.

qa.q: How might Aparna see Noor's charts?
qa.a: Aparna admires them at first, then seems gently curious and supportive when Noor admits nothing is ticked.

grounding: A teenager realises she makes lovely study plans because planning feels like progress, while the chapters stay unread.

subtype: Approach: builds a detailed plan for months ahead and delays starting [Pitfall]
passage:
Week 1
Gopika: Making the ULTIMATE semester timetable. Every hour, every subject, colour-coded 🌈
Vasudha: Have you started the readings?
Gopika: After the timetable. It needs to be perfect first.

Week 2
Gopika: Almost done. Added revision slots, exam weeks, even laundry
Vasudha: Did you do the circuits assignment?
Gopika: It's on the timetable for next week!

Week 3
Gopika: Timetable done. Printed and laminated
Gopika: Started studying today. Omg I'm already 3 chapters behind
Vasudha: The class is on chapter 5
Gopika: The timetable doesn't account for being behind 😩
Vasudha: Maybe just start from where the class is?
Gopika: I spent two weeks on a plan and now the plan is wrong

qa.q: How long did Gopika spend making the timetable?
qa.a: Two weeks; it was done in week 3.

qa.q: How does Gopika feel in week 3?
qa.a: Gopika feels frustrated and panicky, being three chapters behind with a plan that no longer fits.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it now?
qa.a: Planning replaced studying for two weeks; starting from where the class is, with a simple weekly plan, would help more than a perfect one.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see Gopika's timetable?
qa.a: Vasudha seems doubtful from the start, gently asking about the readings and the assignment.

grounding: A student spends two weeks colour-coding a semester timetable before starting, and ends up with less time than before.

subtype: Approach: builds a detailed plan for months ahead and delays starting [Pitfall]
passage: In the district college in Hoshiarpur, the semester started on 1 August. Madhuri decided she would plan everything first. She bought chart paper, three colours of pen and a ruler. For fourteen days, every evening, she drew. Every lecture, every chapter, every revision slot, every mock test until December. Her brother Nitin kept peeping in. "Have you opened a book yet?" "Once the plan's done," she said. On 15 August the plan went up on the wall. It was beautiful. The next morning, Madhuri opened her economics book and found the class had already covered four chapters. The first internal test was in nine days. She stared at the plan. It hadn't counted the two weeks it had taken to make.

qa.q: When did the plan go up on the wall?
qa.a: On 15 August.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she stared at the plan?
qa.a: She likely felt dismayed and anxious, seeing she was four chapters behind with a test in nine days.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were Madhuri?
qa.a: Plan only the first week in rough, start reading the same day, and fill in the plan as the semester goes.

qa.q: How might Nitin see his sister's plan?
qa.a: Nitin seems doubtful and teasing, suspecting the planning was taking the place of studying.

grounding: A student spends two weeks colour-coding a timetable for the whole semester and only then starts studying, with less time left.

subtype: Approach: starts a rough version early to learn what matters [Revision]
passage: Tanuja, sit. You're making a plan for your plan again, aren't you? Let me tell you about your Hemant Mama at nineteen. I had a design project: a model of a bus stop for my architecture class. For ten days I made lists, sketches of sketches, a schedule for each part. I hadn't cut a single piece of card. My professor walked past and said, "Build something ugly by tonight." I was annoyed, but I did it. One afternoon, card and glue, very rough. And that ugly model taught me more than ten days of lists. The roof needed real planning; it kept sagging. The benches didn't; they were simple. So I planned the roof carefully and built the rest quickly. Finished on time.

qa.q: What was young Hemant's design project?
qa.a: A model of a bus stop for an architecture class.

qa.q: How did young Hemant feel when the professor said to build something ugly?
qa.a: He felt annoyed at first, but was willing to try it anyway.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Building a rough model in one afternoon; it showed that the roof needed careful planning and the benches didn't.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt seeing the ugly model?
qa.a: The professor was probably pleased that Hemant finally built something to learn from.

grounding: An elder recalls stopping planning, building a rough draft in one afternoon, and seeing which parts needed planning and which did not.

subtype: Approach: starts a rough version early to learn what matters [Revision]
passage: The hackathon ended at 6 pm, and at 1 pm Ujjwal was still drawing boxes on the whiteboard: screens, buttons, database tables, a colour scheme. Hrithik, his teammate, looked at the clock and groaned. "Five hours left and we have zero code." Ujjwal kept drawing. Then the power flickered and the whiteboard marker died. In the sudden quiet, Ujjwal put it down. "Okay. New plan. We build the ugliest version possible in the next two hours. Just one screen that works." They hacked it together, no colours, no logo. At three they tested it. The login part broke constantly; the list screen was fine. "So login needs real planning," Ujjwal said. "The rest doesn't." They spent the last hours on login and submitted at 5:52.

qa.q: When did the team submit?
How did Ujjwal seem to feel when the marker died?
qa.a: He seemed to snap out of it, suddenly clear-headed and a bit relieved to stop planning.

qa.q: Why did the rough version help the team?
qa.a: It showed that only the login needed careful planning, so they spent their last hours where it mattered.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel at 1 pm?
qa.a: Hrithik felt anxious and frustrated, seeing five hours left and no code.

grounding: Under time pressure, a student stops planning and builds a rough version in an afternoon, which shows which parts needed planning.

subtype: Approach: plans every hour and cannot adapt when things change [Pitfall]
passage:
"Pankaj, did you see my trip plan? It's colour-coded by minute."
"Minute? Rehana, it's a two-day conference."
"7:05 cab. 7:40 airport. 9:15 land. 9:50 hotel. 10:10 first session."
Two days later, at the airport:
"Pankaj, the flight's delayed three hours."
"Okay. So you miss the morning session. Not a disaster."
"But then the lunch meeting is off. And the afternoon session. And the dinner. It all depends on the one before."
"So skip the first session and go straight to lunch?"
"I don't know! There's no plan for this." Her voice was shaking.
"Rehana, breathe. Just call the lunch contact."
"I don't have a backup. Everything was in that sheet."
She sat down on her suitcase, staring at her phone.

qa.q: How long was the flight delayed?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she sat down on her suitcase?
qa.a: She felt lost and panicky; the minute-by-minute plan had broken and she had no backup.

qa.q: What could Rehana do differently for the next trip?
qa.a: Plan the fixed points, like the lunch meeting, and leave loose time between them, so one delay doesn't break everything.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see the delay compared with Rehana?
qa.a: Pankaj sees it as a small problem with easy fixes, while Rehana sees the whole trip falling apart.

grounding: A young manager's minute-by-minute trip plan breaks with a flight delay, and she feels lost without it.

subtype: Approach: plans every hour and cannot adapt when things change [Pitfall]
passage: I still wince when I think of my first conference trip as a team manager. I'm Harsha. I had a spreadsheet: every hour of the two days in Chennai planned, even "12:20–12:35: coffee and networking." My colleague Mohit teased me about it. Then my morning flight was cancelled. The next one would land at three. I sat at the gate and felt the ground go. My talk slot, my meeting with the client, the dinner: in my head they were one chain, and the first link was gone. I didn't call anyone for twenty minutes. I just stared at the sheet. Mohit finally rang me: "The organisers can move your talk. Call them." It had never occurred to me. The plan had become the trip.

qa.q: When would the next flight land?
qa.a: At three.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling at the gate?
qa.a: Harsha felt lost and frozen, as if the ground went, unable to act for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What else could Harsha have done straight away?
qa.a: Call the organisers and the client to rearrange, focusing on the most important item instead of the whole chain.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt when making that call?
qa.a: Mohit was probably worried and wanted to help, suggesting a simple fix Harsha hadn't seen.

grounding: A young manager's minute-by-minute conference plan collapses after a flight cancellation, leaving the planner lost without it.

subtype: Approach: plans the next step in detail and leaves later steps loose [Revision]
passage: Every Monday for a month, Ines had made a detailed plan for the whole month at the architecture firm in Lisbon: tasks by day, hours by task. Every Wednesday it cracked. A client changed a drawing, a site visit moved, and she spent Thursday redoing the entire plan. Her colleague Chidi watched her rewrite the chart for the fourth time. "You plan the month like you can see it," he said. Ines stopped. He was right. She could see about a week clearly; after that, it was fog. So she changed her method. Each Monday, a detailed plan for that week only. For the weeks after that, three rough goals on a sticky note. The next Wednesday a client changed a drawing again. She adjusted two lines and went back to work.

qa.q: How many times had Ines rewritten the chart when Chidi spoke?
qa.a: The fourth time.

qa.q: What did Ines feel when she stopped at Chidi's comment?
qa.a: She felt a flash of recognition and some relief, seeing he was right and the problem was the method, not her effort.

qa.q: What makes the new method better?
qa.a: Detailed plans only for the week she can see clearly, with rough goals later, so changes cost two lines instead of a whole rewrite.

qa.q: How might Chidi see the change?
qa.a: Chidi is likely pleased his comment helped and glad to see Ines less stressed on Thursdays.

grounding: Noticing her plan cracks each week, she plans in detail only for the coming week and keeps rough goals for the rest of the month.

subtype: Approach: plans the next step in detail and leaves later steps loose [Revision]
passage: In the hospital's quality office, Jyoti's month-long audit plan had fallen apart again by the second week. A ward postponed its inspection, a meeting was added, and her colour-coded chart was wrong. Akash, the data analyst who shared the office, found her re-drawing it on Friday evening. "That's the third time," he said. Jyoti put the pen down. "Because I keep planning what I can't know yet." She tore out a fresh page. At the top: "This week: detailed." She listed Monday to Friday, ward by ward, hour by hour. Below: "Rest of month: rough goals." Four lines. Finish ICU audit. Draft report. Two ward visits. Present to committee. The following Wednesday a ward cancelled. Jyoti moved one line.

qa.q: How many rough goals did Jyoti list for the rest of the month?
qa.a: Four lines: finish ICU audit, draft report, two ward visits, present to committee.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when she put the pen down?
qa.a: She seemed frustrated but suddenly clear, seeing she kept planning what she couldn't know yet.

qa.q: What else could Jyoti do to make the plan even steadier?
qa.a: Review the rough goals each Friday and turn only the next week into detail, as the plan now suggests.

qa.q: How does Akash see Jyoti's planning?
qa.a: Akash notices the repeated redrawing and seems gently concerned, prompting her to rethink.

grounding: Noticing her plan cracks each week, she plans in detail only for the coming week and keeps rough goals for the rest of the month.

subtype: Approach: believes a wish or a ritual will cause the result [Thinking]
passage: I'm Arohi, Vikas's big sister. Before every football match in the colony park, Vikas wears his red T-shirt. He says it's lucky. "If I wear it, we win." Last Sunday it had a big mud stain from the week before. Mummy said, "Wear the blue one today." Vikas shook his head hard. "No! Red makes us win!" He hid the red shirt under his pillow so it wouldn't go in the wash. He wore it, stain and all. His team lost two–nil. Vikas sat on the steps, sad. Then he said, "Maybe it needs washing to work again." He still won't wear the blue one.

qa.q: What did Vikas hide under his pillow?
qa.a: His red T-shirt, so it wouldn't go in the wash.

qa.q: Why did Vikas refuse the blue T-shirt?
qa.a: He believed the red shirt made his team win, and felt worried that wearing another would make them lose.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Vikas gently?
qa.a: She could wash the red shirt and talk about how the team wins by passing and practising, not by what anyone wears.

qa.q: How might Arohi see her brother's lucky shirt?
qa.a: Arohi seems fond and a little amused, telling the story kindly.

grounding: A child believes his lucky red shirt makes his team win and refuses to change it even when it is dirty.

subtype: Approach: believes a wish or a ritual will cause the result [Thinking]
passage:
Friday: Nitin wore his red shirt to the school sports day. His team won the relay. "It's my lucky shirt!" he told Mumma Irawati.

Sunday: The shirt had juice on the front. Mumma held out a clean yellow one. Nitin folded his arms. "No. Red makes us win." He wore the sticky red shirt to the park game.

Tuesday: Before class races, Mumma said, "It's in the wash." Nitin cried. "Now we'll lose!" He ran anyway. His team came second. He looked at his yellow shirt, puzzled. "Second is still good," he said slowly.

qa.q: What did Nitin's team win on Friday?
qa.a: The relay, at the school sports day.

qa.q: What did Nitin believe about the red shirt?
qa.a: He believed it made his team win, so he felt scared they would lose without it.

qa.q: What small step could Mumma try next?
qa.a: Praise how fast Nitin ran on Tuesday, so he links the result to his running, not the shirt.

qa.q: What would change if Mumma had let Nitin wear the dirty shirt again on Tuesday?
qa.a: He would keep believing in the shirt, and miss seeing that his team still did well without it.

grounding: A child believes his lucky red shirt makes his team win and refuses to change it even when it is dirty.

subtype: Approach: hopes that it will somehow work out without acting [Pitfall]
passage: In the village of Wai, the class project on local birds was due on Monday. Mehak knew about it for three weeks. Every evening she said, "Tomorrow." Her brother Vishal asked on Wednesday, "Have you started your bird chart?" "It'll be fine," she said, and went to play. On Friday she thought, "Maybe Sir will give more days. He did once, last year." On Sunday night, after dinner, she spread out chart paper under the tube light. She had no pictures, no notes, and the shop was shut. She drew three crooked birds and wrote their names. Her eyes stung. On Monday, Sir didn't extend the date. He collected the charts. Mehak handed in hers without looking up.

qa.q: When was the bird project due?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling on Sunday night?
qa.a: She was panicky and upset; her eyes stung when she saw she had no pictures, no notes and the shop was shut.

qa.q: What could Mehak do differently next time?
qa.a: Start with one small part the first week, like collecting pictures, instead of hoping the date will move.

qa.q: How might Vishal see what happened?
qa.a: Vishal, who asked her on Wednesday, may feel sorry for her and a little worried.

grounding: A girl leaves her project to the last night, telling herself it will be fine and hoping the teacher will extend the date.

subtype: Approach: hopes that it will somehow work out without acting [Pitfall]
passage: In Istanbul, Ada's science project on how plants drink water was due on Thursday. She had two weeks. Her friend Elif started hers on day one, with celery sticks in coloured water. Ada watched and thought, "I'll do mine later. It's easy." On the weekend she went to her cousin's. "Maybe the teacher will give us an extra week," she told herself. "She's kind." On Wednesday night she finally put celery in water, but it needed a day to change colour. She stared at the glass until bedtime. On Thursday morning the celery was only faintly pink. The teacher did not extend the date. Ada handed in half a poster, and her cheeks burned when she saw Elif's bright stalks.

qa.q: What did Elif use for her project?
qa.a: Celery sticks in coloured water.

qa.q: How did Ada feel about the deadline on the weekend?
qa.a: Ada was hopeful the kind teacher would give an extra week, which let her feel relaxed instead of starting.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Ada waited until the last night for an experiment that needed a day; starting early, like Elif, would give it time to work.

qa.q: How might Elif feel seeing Ada's half poster?
qa.a: Elif might feel sorry for Ada, and a little awkward that her own project looked so bright beside it.

grounding: A girl leaves her project to the last night, telling herself it will be fine and hoping the teacher will extend the date.
